subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment last night I was stressing the point that during a depression we cannot hope to expand the purchasing power of the people by financing government expenditures through an expansion of taxation, especially an expansion of taxation upon people in the lower income brackets or of the sales tax or by borrowing from the
The Bank Act
savings of the people because that procedure is bound to reduce their purchasing power to the extent of their borrowing. We insist that it must be done at least in part by monetary expansion.
At the present time we are on a managed currency; and I would say it is a fully managed currency. We in this group support that policy. We have been a managed currency since the year 1940. Prior to that time, for a number of years, we were on what might be called a semi-managed currency; that is, we were on a gold parity although we were not on the gold standard. I would say that the real test of the efficiency of the government's management of currency has yet to come. Ever since 1940 we have had a high level of economic activity, largely as a result of the war; in the post-war period it has been largely as the result of consequences arising out of the war.
In the past the Minister of Finance has supported the general principle of cyclical budgeting. I think we will all agree that during the past few years he has not hesitated to budget for a substantial surplus. I think perhaps there was a good deal of logic in that action because during those years we had a high level of economic activity and we had present strong inflationary pressures. It therefore might be said that it was necessary to withdraw a certain amount of the redundant money from circulation in order to reduce the inflationary pressure.
But whilst I would agree that there was probably a certain amount of justification for that action, I would also point out that in the future, for the same reason, it may be necessary to budget for a deficit. What I mean by that is that if we have a condition where economic activity is falling off and where we are getting into a depressed condition, then the government must be prepared to budget for a deficit. In other words, if a system of equitable taxation and moderate borrowings from the savings of the people fails to provide the government with the money that is necessary to finance their program, then they will have to be prepared to indulge in a certain degree of monetary expansion.

It is quite evident that they have substantial amounts in their reserves at the present time, and we can rest assured that the contingent reserves are adequate to take care of the writing down of any of their published assets. It is interesting to note also that they do not have to pay any income tax when they transfer earnings to that inner reserve.
I believe the figures I have quoted are enough to show that the banks are in a very prosperous condition. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), referring to the banks, said that they were drowning in liquidity. I think that was a poor analogy. I would say that the banks are floating luxuriously on that liquidity. Moreover, they are supported by the government in that floating because there are a number of measures under which the losses of the chartered banks are guaranteed by the government up to a certain percentage. As I say, from the figures I have quoted it is quite evident the chartered banks are doing very well. I feel we would all agree it is highly desirable that they should be doing well, and that they should' be in a sound position.
Just so long as economic activity continues at a high level, there is every reason to believe that the banks of this country will continue to prosper. Therefore, I see no reason why the chartered banks should not be required to service additional deposits arising from government expenditures that are made to maintain a high level of economic activity without any additional compensation for that service. After all, those deposits would only represent a small percentage of the total deposits which are represented by loans and investments that bear interest. I would say that such a service could well be regarded as a premium paid by the chartered banks to help assure

a high level of economic activity in the country, which would assure them a continued prosperous condition.
The chartered banks in Canada today are in a very preferred position. Many of their risks are safeguarded by the government and their profits practically assured. Therefore, the argument by the Bank of Canada that financing through the Bank of Canada would be too hard upon the chartered banks does not, I think, hold water.
In closing I should like to say a few words about the C.C.F. amendment. The leader of this group has already spoken on it. I would agree that if the chartered banks refused to co-operate fully in carrying out government policy, if they were in an unsound position or if they were operating inefficiently, then there might be justification for nationalization. It has been argued that the chartered banks have operated inefficiently at times in the past from the point of view of the borrower. Reference has been made to what happened in the thirties. The chartered banks refused to make loans to farmers and other organizations. As I pointed out in my speech yesterday, the chartered banks at that time were in reality the victims of circumstances. It was the result of the failure of the government of the day to maintain the economic activity of this country at a high level that few loans were made to industry to extend their production. What use is it to make loans to industry to expand production when they were not able to sell their present level of production? A lot of the criticism levelled against the chartered banks should rightfully have been made against the government's economic and financial policies.
On the other hand, if it is argued that profits are too great, there are many ways in which parliament can take action to limit those profits. I have shown one method by which the chartered banks could provide a greater service to the people of Canada, and of course to the extent that they did that their profits would be reduced.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said yesterday in opening the debate on second reading, Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 338 is a measure that is important but not controversial. One might have expected that a measure of this kind being largely technical would give rise to only a short debate. The amendments that the minister catalogued in his speech yesterday are not far-reaching. There are a half a dozen of them that merit mention, but broadly speaking there is no far-reaching revision of the Bank Act contemplated this year.

The amendments will have the effect of increasing the minimum cash reserve required on the part of the banks from 5 per cent to 8 per cent of their Canadian dollar deposit liabilities; the banks will be for the first time in Canadian banking history given the power to lend on the security of mortgages on real estate, through the medium of insured loans provided for in the new housing act which was passed through this chamber and given third reading yesterday. The other amendments are not of an extensive nature. Provision is made for facilitating loans on the part of banks for the development of the oil reserves of this country. There is a slight amendment to the important section 88 in relation to loans in the case of seed potatoes. There is a prohibition which has been expected for a long time against the issuance of notes in circulation and a provision for doubling the capital requirement on the part of new banks, both as to subscribed and issued capital.
There is nothing in amendments of this kind, Mr. Speaker, that would give rise to an extensive debate on second reading. However, the leader of the C.C.F., on behalf of his party, yesterday introduced an amendment that I think should engage the serious attention of the house. The amendment, as it is recorded on page 2778 of Hansard for March 8, 1954, reads as follows:
That Bill No. 338 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the national ownership and public control of the chartered banks.
I welcome the introduction of this amendment. I do not welcome it because I am prepared to give any support to it or because it finds any degree of favour in my eyes. I welcome it, Mr. Speaker, for several reasons.
It may help to relieve something of the tedium of dull debate in a session that has, as a whole, been rather dull-although I do not pretend to confound contention with constructiveness, or to say that dullness is always the test of constructiveness. But I do welcome it, principally because there is revealed in this amendment an element of self-exposure on the part of the socialist party which, I think, is timely.
We have seen over a period of years a change of doctrine on the part of the C.C.F. from time to time. Perhaps some of them will think that is a harsh way of putting it. I think it has gone much beyond mere changes in emphasis. Those of us who have watched them in the house over a period of years have seen very pronounced changes in the doctrines espoused by the socialist party in the House of Commons. Some of
The Bank Act
these changes have been attributable, of course, to changes in personnel of that party in the house. For instance we recall that after certain by-elections in June of 1948, with the entry of several-two in particular-new members of the socialist party into this house, there was a definite leftist turn in the flavour of C.C.F. speeches. After the rebuke administered by the electorate to that party in 1949 we find them rather shrinking away from the tendencies which had been evident previously, and becoming more cautious and moderate. Indeed it reached the point where one hon. member of that party, then representing the riding of Moose Jaw, began to make speeches which by no stretch of the imagination could possibly be reconciled with the doctrines which had been espoused by the party to which he gave outward adherence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries

speechtext: You are so right.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: And, coming to the present parliament, we have seen some evidence again of a tendency to shift left, with the accession to the C.C.F. membership in the house of some whose views appear to be considerably to the left of those who sat as representatives of that party in the twenty-first parliament of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would you like to tell us who they are?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. member does not know, then I suggest he has not been spending his time to very good advantage.
Mr. Speaker, in this amendment we see the C.C.F. back at Regina. The leopard has not changed his spots. Notwithstanding the shifts of emphasis and the shifts of policy we have seen in the socialist party in recent years, they are right back at Regina. And we have waited-I think some of us with interest-for evidence that the C.C.F. stands firmly where it stood when its Regina manifesto was written in 1933.
Now, may I ask the house to put side by side the amendment introduced in this house yesterday with this extract from the Regina manifesto of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation adopted in July of 1933. Under the heading "Socialization of Finance" we find this subheading:
Socialization of all financial machinery-banking, currency, credit, and insurance, to make possible the effective control of currency, credit and prices, and the supplying of new productive equipment for socially desirable purposes.
And then this paragraph proceeds:
Planning by itself will be of little use if the public authority has not the power to carry its

The Bank Act
plans into effect. Such power will require the control of finance and of all those vital industries and services, which, if they remain in private hands, can be used to thwart or corrupt the will of the public authority. Control of finance is the first step in the control of the whole economy. The chartered banks must be socialized and removed from the control of private profit-seeking interests; and the national banking system thus established must have at its head a central bank to control the flow of credit and the general price level, and to regulate foreign exchange operations. A national investment board must also be set up, working in co-operation with the socialized banking system to mobilize and direct the unused surpluses of production for socially desired purposes as determined by the planning commission.
Insurance companies, which provide one of the main channels for the investment of individual savings and which, under their present competitive organization, charge needlessly high premiums for the social services that they render, must also be socialized.
Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. has marched now, for all to see, right back to Regina. There had been suggestions previously that the C.C.F. had turned its back on Regina. Indeed, Mr. Donald C. MacDonald, then national director of organization for the C.C.F. party, and now the provincial leader for that party in Ontario, on March 8, 1951, had occasion to object to interpretations placed upon decisions taken by the C.C.F. national council in that month of March 1951, and which had been widely commented upon by the press and public of this country. He was trying to reassure the public in a letter to the press, in which he said:
In the second place the C.C.F. national convention did not reject the Regina manifesto.
Well, on that occasion, if it refrained from rejecting it, it certainly did not say anything about the nationalization of the banks. Indeed, in other pronouncements from the C.C.F. it has been extraordinary that such a degree of silence has been observed on what was regarded in 1933 by the C.C.F. as something of such high importance that it found second place in the list of far-reaching planks written by that party into its platform.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I welcome this selfexposure on the part of the C.C.F. as to its true designs on the Canadian economy.
There is one sentence in the Regina manifesto, in the paragraph from which I have just read, which is absolutely correct. And it is so correct that I hope all members of the house, and the Canadian public, will realize its significance. That sentence is:
Control of finance is the first step in the control of the whole economy.
And, Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. in proposing, as they are in this present amendment, the national ownership and public control of the chartered banks in Canada, is inviting the

House of Commons to take what they regard as the first step toward the control of the whole economy. Well, for my part, I wish to record as emphatic opposition as any I am capable of to this proposal.
It was a weak case, indeed, that the leader of the C.C.F. offered yesterday in support of this radical and sweeping proposal, such a case that it is not to be justified by expressions such as he used yesterday in describing the banking system as "an instrument of monetary policy". Mr. Speaker, to say that is a far cry from a proposal for the nationalization of the chartered banks of Canada. Indeed, if they are looking for avenues for undertaking whatever monetary and fiscal controls are necessary over the banking system of Canada, then what is the Bank of Canada for? A case could rarely have been weaker than the one put forward yesterday by the leader of the C.C.F.
Now, I wish to make this observation about the Canadian banking system in general. The Canadian banking system is unique in all the world. It is not just like any other banking system in the world. There are some who trace some aspects of it to Scottish sources and others to American sources. The fact is that the Canadian banking system has elements which are absolutely unique the world over. It is a system that has been tested. It is a system that has been submitted to very severe testing-and indeed probably the most severe within the lifetime of every member in the house. And no banking system in the world emerged from the acid test of the depression of the 1930's with a better record, or in a stronger or more healthy position, than the Canadian banking system. Much of that health of course is attributable to the fact that it is a system built upon branches. In that respect it has differed so much from the system in vogue in the United States. That branch system has drawn its strength from the whole far-flung economy of Canada.
It is so easy for hon. members to the left to picture the banks as if they were the enemies of the economy, as though all the ills in the economy were to be attributed to the banks. Mr. Speaker, anyone who knows anything about the banking system, or has studied the history of the Canadian banking system, well knows that in general what is good for business in Canada-and that goes for all aspects of the Canadian economy, our primary industries as well as secondary industries-is good also for the banks. The banks cannot prosper when the Canadian economy is stagnant or receding.
Sir, this banking system is such that there has been no failure of a chartered bank now

for more than 30 years. We do not want any more bank failures; we do not want such tinkering by theorists with the Canadian banking system as in any measure to jeopardize the soundness of that system, because the effects of the failure of a chartered bank extend far beyond the interests of its depositors, its creditors and its shareholders. That was so in connection with the last bank failure in Canada, the Home Bank. The effects of that failure extended very far into the Canadian economy. And, Mr. Speaker, we do not want in this house, I believe, to do anything that is going to subtract from the strength of this system. It is a system that has grown in strength and in public confidence.
Those factors do not occur by accident, Mr. Speaker. You cannot find any more effective tribute to the soundness of the Canadian banking system, or to the way in which it has served the banking needs of the Canadian people, than the fact that the system has grown stronger and that with it has grown the public's confidence in it. Indeed the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) felt called upon to recognize the service and what he called the impressive record of the Canadian banking system. At page 2772 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
I am going to say at once that the Canadian banks have a very impressive record of efficient management, of safety-
And then of course he added:
-and of profit to their shareholders.
Well, let us take that statement as we find it. It is at least a recognition of the banks' impressive record, in the way in which they have served the needs of the Canadian economy. Sir, yesterday the Minister of Finance, in opening his speech, used these words, at page 2761 of Hansard:
. . . there is general agreement that within the framework of our accepted economic structure our banking system is an excellent system; that it is efficient; it gives good service; it commands the confidence of the Canadian people; and it is highly regarded abroad.
Let me say at once that in so gauging the opinion of this house he certainly spoke for me, because those sentiments I do most heartily echo.
Let it not be forgotten, sir, that the Canadian banking system is a competitive one. That is one of the reasons for the strength of the Canadian banking system. It has been a system based upon keen competition. And in the last analysis, sir, its strength rests upon the way in which it has served the Canadian people; for businesses and individuals in this country from one end of it to the
The Bank Act
other have owed so much to the advice and guidance they have received at the hands of their bankers.
But we have attacks made, sir, on the Canadian banks. We have attempts on the part of socialists in this house to blame the banking system for all the ills of the country. Everything that is wrong can be laid at the door of the banks: such is their reasoning. Well, let us be fair about this. Let us recognize in the first place that limitations are imposed upon the business of banking; they are imposed by statute of this parliament of Canada and they are imposed also by sound common sense.
Banking is important; it is a factor of the highest importance in relation to our own economy; but it is not the only factor in the Canadian economy. And I cannot agree with those in this house who say that the regulation of the volume of bank deposits is the dominant factor in determining the strength of the Canadian economy. Sir, those who think along that line would do well to recall what Mr. Graham Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada, has had to say before some of the committees in this house in recent years in commenting upon the preamble to the Bank of Canada Act. Let me remind the house of the provisions of the preamble:
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion.
Mr. Graham Towers has had occasion more than once to shake his head before committees of this house when faced with that preamble and to question how the Bank of Canada could be expected to fulfil all the objects set forth therein. It is perhaps time that the house measured a little more realistically the possible scope within which even the central banking facilities of this country may operate.
And the second limitation, Mr. Speaker, is the sound and legitimate limitation against the taking of unhealthy risks. It seems that when anybody has some pet project, if the banks do not lend money upon it, that is fair occasion for denunciation of the banks. Let us remember, Mr. Speaker, that the powers of the banks are limited by law and many risks the banks and others are called upon to take are unwise, and in shrinking from

The Bank Act
those risks the banks are following the sound practice of protecting the deposits that are placed in their hands.
We heard criticism in this house yesterday of the fact that parliament had intervened in such measures as the setting up of the industrial development bank, in the provision of farm improvement loans, home improvement and extension loans and in the insuring of loans under the National Housing Act, and has underwritten risks which private enterprise and the chartered banks ought to be accepting.
Well, Mr. Speaker, who says that the banks ought to be accepting those risks? Surely, Mr. Speaker, those who are charged with the responsibility of administering funds placed in their hands, funds largely emanating in the first place from deposits in their hands, must be very calculating in their assumption of risks with money that after all, in the last analysis, does not strictly belong to them.
In reference to all these measures, why do the socialists in this house not be fair and say that the banks were pushed into loans of these kinds, were urged to embark upon fields which were foreign to their experience because it was public policy on the part of this parliament to encourage the banks to enter those fields? We had evidence just the other day-I am not going to comment on this at length-of the position of the banks in reference to the extension of their powers into new investment in insured loans on the security of real estate.
This is a new field, brand new to the banks. They say they do not know anything about it, and they would not have chosen to be in it. They did not ask to go into it. They are put in that field today only because it becomes public policy on the part of parliament to give them powers to go into that field.
In all these measures, Mr. Speaker, whether it is insured loans, home improvement and extension loans or the industrial development bank, it was the decision on the part of parliament that the banks go into a field which was largely at that time beyond the range of banking policy. It is quite proper in these cases, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, when parliament is prodding the banks to take risks in new fields, and where substantial risks are involved, that parliament, if it takes the course of following what is considered to be sound public policy, should be prepared to facilitate those steps.
Let us look at experience elsewhere. The experience of other nations in this respect is interesting but we do not have to go beyond the experience of the United Kingdom. When

the socialists came into power in the United Kingdom in 1945 they had ample opportunity -no government ever had more-to take every step they wished in the direction of nationalization of the joint stock banks of that country; but when Labour went out of power at the end of 1951 they had not nationalized a single joint stock bank in the United Kingdom-not one. What more proof do you need that nationalization of banks is an imprudent and reckless course? The Labour party today in Britain is not making any proposals along the lines the C.C.F. party in this parliament has undertaken to put forward and espouse in this amendment.
I wish to examine, in the time that remains, what I consider to be the certain effects of nationalization of the Canadian banking system, if such a course were ever undertaken.
The first result would be to drive confidence away. Sir, you cannot have capital available for needed investment unless there is confidence. It was Lenin who said that all you needed to destroy the political system of the west, or democracy, was to have a series of recurring depressions. I am not sure he was altogether right, Mr. Speaker, but at any rate it remains a fact that if you destroy confidence then you certainly can destroy an economy, because a free economy depends upon confidence.
What are the sources of capital in an economy such as ours? The first source is profits, that much-maligned word, that word which is thrown around as though there was something inherently wicked about profits. I am not going to condone profits which are improperly made or are excessive. I am here to say, however, without fear of contradiction, that profits are absolutely essential to our free economy, and if there are not going to be profits there is not going to be national development, nor will there be the capital for the development of these great resources of Canada.
When our friends to the left decry the profits which the banks made in recent years, let us not forget the years when the banks, like other institutions, were not making profits, and when business was finding it difficult to succeed. Let us not forget also that in this prosperity the exchequer of the Canadian government is the principal shareholder.
The second source of capital is from abroad. One reason for the strength of the Canadian economy has been that it has given rise to confidence abroad, and no one factor has contributed more to the feeling of confidence abroad in the Canadian economy than has

the Canadian banking system. Indeed, that was recognized only last week in a speech made by President Gordon R. Ball of the Bank of Montreal when he said that the increasing foreign investment at stake in Canadian industry is an accumulating benefit to the nation. I would like to quote from a BUP dispatch of the speech made by Mr. Ball at Montreal on March 2. The report states:
The foreign stake in Canada has increased by $3 billion since 1945 to more than $10 billion at the end of 1952, Mr. Ball said. The increase, compared with $30 billion of new Canadian capital expenditure in eight years, represents less than 8 per cent of Canada's post-war spending of a capital nature.
Mr. Ball referred to Canada's oil industry as "a world industry," and he said it was to be expected that much of the stimulus to explore and develop the potentialities of the Canadian west should come from United States companies.
Of all United States foreign investment, Mr. Ball said, close to one-third is in Canada, and a considerable part of that came from the re-investment of profits, which made the investment "not a drain but an accumulating benefit."
Of this widening area of United States participation in investment in Canada, Mr. Ball said, "it was a natural development and it should be understood before it is criticized."
If you want to put a stop to the assistance given by foreign capital to the development of Canadian resources, and thereby to the provision of expanding opportunities for Canadian youth and workmen, then all you need to do is to support measures of the kind envisaged in this C.C.F. amendment. There can be no surer way of destroying confidence abroad in Canada's economy than to carry out the proposal made for the nationalization of the Canadian chartered banks.
Even the effect of speeches such as the kind which have been made by C.C.F. members in this debate has been harmful on this occasion, as on past occasions, when they affect that confidence.
The second result of nationalization would be a breakdown. There is not enough wisdom in any government to operate a banking monopoly in Canada. A year or so ago I heard the present Chancellor of the Exchequer in the United Kingdom, Mr. R. A. Butler, make this comment in the House of Commons at Westminster in reference to a measure taken by the government. He said: "The view of the government is that businessmen best know how to run business." By the same token, may I express my view that the bankers of this country, reputable, competent and highly respectable, best know how to operate the banking system of this country. One would imagine, listening to some of the speeches made in this house, that anyone without the slightest experience in banking, 83276-178
The Bank Act
or even in managing a business-with one sole exception in a certain party-could step in and manage not just a branch of a bank, not just one entire chartered bank, but all the banks in Canada. To reduce the position to terms such as that, Mr. Speaker, is to expose its utter absurdity. I do not know how many hon. members in this house have had personal experience in relation to banking in Canada. I doubt very much if there are many. Perhaps you could count them on the fingers of both hands. But I am perfectly certain, sir, that they are not to be found among those who are advocating nationalization of the Canadian banks. It seems to me that the less experience they have of the banking business the more freely they talk of taking the banks over and running them through some little cabal here in Ottawa.
The third result of nationalization would be an end of competition in our Canadian banking system, and with the end of competition would come the end of a factor which has been one of the greatest contributing factors to the strength of the Canadian banking system.
The next result would be regimentation. That is quite clear, and all one requires to do is to refer to that clear-cut and accurately expressed sentence in the Regina manifesto to which I alluded earlier, namely: "Control of finance is the first step in the control of the whole economy."
If those who are advocating nationalization of the banks had the right and the power to plunge this country into that course, you know perfectly well, Mr. Speaker, it would be the first step to complete socialization and the foisting upon the Canadian economy of socialistic regimentation-the inevitable accompaniment of socialism.
The fifth result, sir, would be centralization of power over the entire Canadian economy right here in Ottawa. Centralization of economic and political power has been the inevitable and invariable accompaniment of socialism. We have seen it in the United Kingdom. We have seen it in other countries where nations have plunged into a socialistic course. For a country like Canada, so widespread in geographical extent, so diversified in its nature, a nation that has every reason to avoid centralization by reason of the duality of cultures, the danger of centralization here at Ottawa of vast powers is an especially threatening peril and one that we must avoid at all risks. Do we wish to see all the bank employees of this country made civil servants? What bank manager, under those circumstances, is going to feel free to impart advice to those who are seeking loans

The Bank Act
from the bank? Being a civil servant, do you think he is going to set himself up to advise the public? That is not the role that is usually chosen by civil servants of their own volition.
When you examine in detail what this proposal would mean, Mr. Speaker, I think it serves to show how little serious thought and serious experience have entered into it. What man is going to go to a civil servant and discuss, in the intimate and confidential way that is customary today between bank customers and bank managers, his pressing private affairs? Under those conditions, I submit that the proposal smacks of absurdity.
The sixth result would be opening the door to political influences. Mr. Speaker, I ask you to think of the function of the branch manager of a socialized bank in dealing with an application for a loan, if political pressure through the local member of parliament or through the local political organization associated with the party to which the government in power belongs were exerted upon him. I contend that you are opening the door to the wrecking of any pretence of soundness in the Canadian banking system. Go further, Mr. Speaker, if you will, and think of the recovery of loans or security on the part of the banks in case of default. Think of the intrusion of political pressures into a situation of that kind. Again you are opening the door, by proposals of this kind, to a complete bedevilling of the whole Canadian economy and any pretence of sound business methods in the Canadian economy.
The seventh result would be to place depositors' funds at the mercy of political pressures and the whims of an oligarchy here at Ottawa. Put this up to the average Canadian. How many of them would wish to entrust their precious savings to the management of those who would be dominated here at Ottawa, if this proposal ever were carried into effect, by long-haired theorists who know jolly little about the operation of the banking system?
I have referred already to the matter of confidence abroad. I say that as an eighth inevitable result, the nationalization of the Canadian banking system would lead at once to the loss of confidence abroad and an end of investment of foreign capital in the development of our Canadian resources.
I submit to this house that the proposal contained in this amendment is just as unsound as any proposal could possibly be. Indeed it is difficult to understand how hon. members of this house could really seriously put forward such a proposal. It is dressed up. It is given, as best that could be done by those who have espoused it, a seductive attraction. But, Mr. Speaker, those who have

put forward this proposal and have urged nationalization of the Canadian banking system are simply singing the siren song of socialism.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having listened to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) for the last 30 or 40 minutes I have come to the conclusion that he is going to vote against our amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: He refuses to be seduced.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As usual, he waxed eloquent, he waxed wrathy and he waxed indignant. I know of nothing in this house against which he does not pour out his indignation. In judging between the various types of indignation, I find great difficulty in ascertaining which is the greater and which is the lesser. I find it difficult to ascertain whether he is more indignant at times against the government for its budgetary policy or its housing policy or against us for introducing into this chamber the subject of nationalization of the banks. However, I should really congratulate him. We appreciate what he did. Yesterday we dangled the bait in front of the supporters of the capitalist system-I refer to the bait of nationalization of the banks-hoping that somebody would gulp it and that we could then have a debate on our own terms. The hon. member for Eglinton has obliged us. I extend an invitation to other members to do exactly the same thing. This is particularly what we want.
The hon. member for Eglinton suddenly found out that we in the C.C.F. had exposed ourselves, that we had become socialists. Here we are coming to the Canadian House of Commons and saying that we want nationalization of the banks. A great light apparently has descended upon my hon. friend. But had he read the amendment we made ten years ago, he would have found that it was much similar in terms. I suppose one could say that being ten years out of date is not too much to expect from a Tory. But he is really twenty years out of date, on his own admission, when he reads to us the Regina manifesto and says, "Here is the C.C.F. actually proposing once again the socialization of the banks". Of course we are. We are doing it, we think, for a good reason. Some of his other arguments I shall take up during the course of my remarks.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: And take apart.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
And perhaps take apart too. Apart from our own amendment, I think one of the most significant amendments was that moved by the government, namely that dealing with the lifting

of the prohibition of loans upon real estate. There has been a distinct change of mind on the part of the government over the last few years. It was just ten years ago when Mr. Ilsley said in parliament that ours has been a banking system of unusual strength, and that this is owing, in part to other causes, but in part to the prohibition of loans upon real estate. So ten years ago this government would have looked askance at such loans. Ten years ago this government would apparently have frowned upon such loans. They appeared to regard them as unsafe. But belatedly there has been a change of opinion on the part of the government and now they regard them as quite acceptable.
Of course it is a dramatic change in policy which the banks themselves do not want. One might perhaps ask this question. Is the government chipping and chiselling away at the foundation of security which these great banking edifices have built? Is the government deliberately trying to weaken the banking system by introducing this legislation? Obviously the answer is no. I would say that the government has come to the conclusion-and again a belated one-that the banks of Canada are not playing their full part in the economy of Canada and so the government is determined to try to induce them to do so. It will be difficult. Banks and bankers, in this country especially, are cautious and conservative. The banks do not like change. They do not want change. They will resist it. They do not desire change. They will oppose it. When change comes along, they oppose changing even change. They are thorough conservatives, to the extent that they are quite prepared to die defending that which their predecessors died opposing.
But why then should there be this amendment? I have a reason with which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) may not altogether agree. I think it is because, to some extent, the banks are being made instruments of government fiscal policy. It is a change which we appreciate because as we see it it is another socialist nail in the coffin of capitalism.
I said that the banks were conservative and cautious. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised all sorts of bogeys as to what other people thought about the banks. As far as we are concerned, we do not underrate or underestimate the part they play in our society and in our economy. The banks perform functions of tremendous importance. In other days I know that the banks were maligned and blamed because they were creators of credit. But I maintain that the creation 83276-1784
The Bank Act
of credit is a necessary business. I maintain that the creation of credit is an honourable business as well as being necessary, and if the creation of credit were to stop then the economic system under which we are living would grind to a sudden and dismal end.
Nevertheless there are certain anomalies in the situation. For instance, the government insists, and rightly so, that the profits from the issue of money, that is, coinage, notes and so on, should revert to the state, and yet it agrees that the profit from the expansion of credit should not. We are told that the creation of money is the prerogative of the state. If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) found somebody else creating money I imagine he would not rest until he had locked up that person for a certain number of years. It is a serious offence for individuals to create money in that sense, and yet it seems to be right and proper for the banks to do it by creating credit.
In view of the fact that the Minister of Finance is going to bring down the budget at some indeterminate time, and in view of the fact that he may be looking for a little extra money with which to satisfy the pressures that bear upon him, I suggest that here is an avenue of taxation. There could be an element of taxation upon this profit arising out of coinage, at the expense of the nation. I do not say these profits are fantastic, far from it, but there is an element of profit there which could well revert to the public treasury.
If the banks are as conservative as I believe them to be, what place is there for them in what is really a young and dynamic society? We are living in a free-enterprise world. It is one in which risks are allegedly taken, one in which we take various chances to achieve our ends. But the banks are not prepared to take risks. The hon. member for Eglinton said that my leader made out a weak case yesterday. He made out a case the purport of which was that the banks today were taking no risks whatsoever. I think it is a case which to some extent is worth repeating. The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) mentioned yesterday the Farm Improvement Loans Act of 1944. The purpose of that measure was to provide short and intermediate credit for the improvement and development of farms. The banks were not coming across. They were not prepared to take any risks whatsoever to give farmers the credit they wanted, and so the government had to step into the picture and introduce the legislation.
As the act says, the purpose of the measure was to assist the average farmer who ordinarily would not be able to obtain bank credit for such proposals. The banks by

The Bank Act
themselves were -unwilling to do it. The banks consented to do it only when the resources of the people of Canada were mobilized through the government and when the banks were told that they would be guaranteed against any possible loss up to 10 per cent of the total loan. Why should the banks not have accepted that risk? The hon. member for Eglinton asked that. Was there any great loss associated with it? History says no. Indeed, I believe the loss was in the neighbourhood of l/100th of 1 per cent up to 1952. Surely this was a risk which private enterprise could have taken, but the capitalist banks refused to undertake it until they were guaranteed by the resources of the people against loss.
There was a suggestion ten years ago that fishermen should receive the same sort of treatment as farmers. At that time the government was prepared to introduce legislation. For its own good reasons it did not do so, but it would be very interesting to find how much money was advanced by the banks to fishermen without the guarantee of the government which was given in the case of the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
In 1937 we had the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act under which the government hoped to create employment to some extent by means of loans issued through the banks to individuals who would use the loans to improve their homes. The banks were not prepared to go ahead with the scheme. Pressure was brought to bear on them by the government, but until the House of Commons again guaranteed the banks against loss, they would risk nothing. What was the measure of risk anyway? I am told that losses under the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act were less than 1 per cent, but before the banks would take the chance of losing 1 per cent they had to be guaranteed up to a total of 10 per cent of the total loans made.
What about the industrial development bank? That was a bank which we started ten years ago because we were told that it would harm the banks' liquidity if they were to undertake loans such as were envisaged under the industrial development bank. What happened? In the last ten years approximately $76 million net in loans has been advanced. That is an average of between $7 million and $8 million a year. Is there any member in the house who would suggest for a moment that $7 million or $8 million so invested each year by the banks would have harmed their liquidity by one iota? Of course not. The banks were not prepared to go ahead and so the government did so. What about the losses under this particular scheme? According to the last

balance sheet I saw losses totalled about $163,000, J of 1 per cent of the net loans or 3 per cent of the entire profit made over the period the industrial development bank was in operation up until last year.
Was this 3 per cent too great a risk for the private banks to undertake? Apparently it was. They did not want to go into the field. Now they are being asked to go into the field of lending money on mortgages. They do not like it. They have told us they do not like it, and I suspect that they feel like sacrificial goats upon the altar of capitalism. But no matter how much or how little blood they exude, the fact remains that they are going to be guaranteed against loss up to 98 per cent. The fact also remains that they are going to be given a very attractive rate of interest-we do not know what yet. I suspect it may be as high as 5J per cent, but if it is 5J per cent then that is akin to usury for what is a gilt-edged investment.
We are told about the liquidity of the banks. In the past that liquidity has been a fetish, but it is now a fetish which is losing some of its sanctity because the government is suggesting that the banks decrease some of their liquidity and put funds into mortgages. Of course the argument of the banks is that they must always be able to meet the demands of their depositors. That is true, but very frequently the banks do not look on the banking situation in Canada as a system. They are inclined to look upon it only from the point of view of their own particular bank. However, when a cheque is withdrawn from one bank then under the system it becomes a deposit in another bank and the system as a whole is not affected.
The deposits of the people of Canada are safe. Let there be no doubt about that. But why do the people know that their deposits are safe? The simple reason is that in the event of any calamity overwhelming a bank the collective resources of the people of Canada through their government would come to the rescue of that bank and the deposits would be more than adequately safeguarded. Their deposits would be secure and are as secure today as government of Canada bonds. The reason is that the government is behind the banks. Of course the government is behind them. The government protects, secures, guarantees and on occasion bails out the banks, as it did in 1931. The banks can pawn, pledge and mortgage without loss; the banks can lend, advance and invest without loss. The banks are protected in making profits. The banks have been guaranteed against losses. Was there ever a welfare state like this? Is there any group

in Canada that is so well protected? Is there any group in Canada that is so well off as this little empire which has been carved out of the Canadian economy? I doubt it.
Obviously, all the banks want is the cream. They are not prepared to take the skim milk. Others can take the risks, but the cream is for them. I do not deny for a moment that skim milk may be nutritive, but one gets tired of it, and perhaps one may aspire to a little cream. The fact is, however, when cream is the sole diet then one becomes fat, lazy and lethargic, a situation in which our banks are already. They are adamant for a riskless industry. So long as the banks are not prepared to play their part in a free enterprise system, the part they are expected to play, I can see no reason for their existence as members of a free enterprise system. Not for a moment do I deny there is competition. I know there is competition between banks, because I have seen it. But I submit that that competition is for business that involves loans, investments and securities which are as riskless as possible.
As I see it, the reason advanced for the existence of free enterprise is the willingness to take risks. The banks are far beyond that stage. They have graduated. They are looking now upon the Canadian economy from a much higher point of view-I will not say from an avuncular point of view, I leave that for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)-but from a paternal point of view. It is not fatherly in the sense that we usually associate with fatherhood, but from a patriarchal point of view. They look upon the Canadian scene through cold, unfeeling eyes. They are against the rashness and wickedness of risktaking. They must be secure in everything they do. For all practical purposes they have immobilized themselves.
We, in the C.C.F., argue that the banks have a far more vital part to play in this country. We argue, from the evidence that has been submitted, that the banks are not prepared to play that part. One of the functions of a banking system is to help to maintain full employment. I do not say for a moment that the banking system can avert depression, but the banking system is ancillary to fiscal policies carried out by the government. It is conceivable that there could be situations in which our bank treasuries were brimming over with money to lend and nobody would want a loan. The demand for loans can only come through the fiscal measures instituted by the government of the country. The demand must be inspired.
There is one matter which has to be remembered, one figure I think which has to be remembered, even in a free enterprise system.
The Bank Act
It is an index figure which should be emblazoned on the minds of the cabinet. It is the index figure of unemployment, because that is the index of the health of the society in which we are living. We do not believe that we can get full employment consistently in a free enterprise system without the ownership and control of the banks.
The government disagrees. The government believes that control can be achieved through the Bank of Canada. Yet, if we are to call history as a witness, the fact remains that in the years from 1935 to 1939, when we had the Bank of Canada and when we can assume it had the powers it needed, nevertheless there was a steady half million of unemployed. Some 25 per cent of our resources were not used. The government had the control. The government had the power, but the government did not give Canada full employment. We have those controls which the government today insists are still adequate.
How adequate would those controls be in a time of declining prices; in a time of pessimism in the market; in a time of financial stringency? It is at that time credit should be expanded. Does the government believe, through the controls it has, it has sufficient power to compel the banks to expand credit at that particular time? Will the banks not be confronted, as they have told us so often in the past, with their obligations to depositors and their obligation to their shareholders? We say that we do not believe those controls will work in such a period of declining prices and pessimistic outlook, therefore the banks have to be nationally owned.
Today the banks in Canada are not only economic factors. They are social factors. They are not only social factors, but they are public utilities. They are to be used for the good of the whole economy. I noticed that the member for Eglinton became very worried today at the idea of nationalization of the banks. He felt there would be political control of the banks. He declares, along with other members, that the banks would not be independent of politics.
What worries me more, and what affects me more, is that politics is not independent of the banks. Whenever the banks are in trouble, whenever they want some security, whenever they want a guarantee, they come to the representatives of the people to bail them out of trouble or get guarantees. The banks are continually interfering with politics so I believe it is high time politics started interfering with the banks and telling them what they have to do.
I said earlier one of the functions of the banks is to help maintain full employment. I am not suggesting that the banks should

The Bank Act
suddenly go in for a rash, unwise expansion of credit. It is not always needed. I believe that even in the capitalist system there is always enough money to buy that which is being produced. In other words, I argue there is no inherent deficiency of purchasing power within the capitalist system. I say that for this reason. Every element of cost in industry, whether it be raw materials, wages, rent, interest or profits, must of necessity be an element in somebody's income. This means that at some stage in the game there is always equilibrium. At some or all stages in the game, the total income must equal the total costs.
The mistake which has been made in the past was the assumption that when that equilibrium was arrived at, it automatically meant there was full employment. It means nothing of the sort, because one could have that type of equilibrium with 10 per cent of our resources used, 50 per cent or 90 per cent. Only at one particular point could we have equilibrium where there is full employment, and that particular point can only be arrived at by conscious planning by the government. This government, which supports free enterprise, opposes conscious planning. Indeed, conscious planning would be the very antithesis of free enterprise. The government can argue that they have, in recent years, achieved' a state of full employment, but it was not by conscious planning. It was, perhaps, due in part to preparing for war; but as a normal, steady situation under a capitalist system full employment can only occur by the most amazing fluke.
Let me go further and assume that equilibrium with full employment and with a total effective demand for 100 units. This would imply total costs would be 100 units. In society as we have it today, 80 of those units might be spent on consumption goods, leaving 20 for savings. Out of that saving, 10 would be expended on capital goods and 10 would be hoarded. This means that there are 90 units available to buy that which costs 100. I need not enlarge upon the economic effects. It means there would be a downward trend in prices. It would mean we were headed to some extent for a depression unless the government were to take remedial action. This analogy does not mean there is insufficient purchasing power within the community. The purchasing power is there, but it is not being used. It is lying dormant, probably in the banks.
The way in which this dormant purchasing power should be taken up is by fiscal measures undertaken by the government. The government can increase consumption,

it can increase investments; or it can do both. But if the government wishes to maintain full employment it has got to take active and remedial steps.
As I said, this means conscious planning. We do not say there is insufficient purchasing power at that stage, but that there is maldistribution of purchasing power. And it is there in part where you find the basis of the socialist case. The money is there, but too few are getting too much of it, while too many are getting too little of it. There is only one way that situation can be alleviated, and that is by taxation and fiscal measures. If we want to make the poor richer, then we have to make the rich poorer. There is no secret way of achieving equality in society except by that sort of redistribution.

speechtext: They have done that in Russia.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, they have not; and you do not know much about Russian economics if you believe that. There is more class distinction in Russia today than there is in Canada.
Our complaint is this. The banking system ought to be prepared to lend, to invest and to take risks, but our banking system is not always prepared to do those things. The commercial banking system ought to be prepared to play a more vital part in the economy of the country, if we are to have full employment and if we are to achieve something which I have no doubt all of us have in mind, the abolition of poverty. And yet recent history gives no guarantee whatsoever that the commercial banks are prepared in any way to take risks. They will not do so without guarantees. Well, if we are going to guarantee the banks in this way would it not be better and quicker just to take them over and do the job ourselves?
We argue that the government must plan consciously for the full use of our resources, and that can be done only, in part, by owning as well as controlling the machinery of credit. After all, the fundamental -case for socialism rests on a policy of removing economic privation and poverty. We maintain that poverty is probably the greatest evil in the world today, the evil from which all other evils spring. Poverty is the impassable barrier to things that give value to human life. Poverty is the lot of far too many in this country. I am not suggesting that nationalization of the banking system will remove it, but I do maintain that nationalization of the banks will be a substantial step forward to this end.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but after listening for two days to a debate in which members of the C.C.F. party have been expounding their socialist views I have thought it necessary to say just a word or two, so that the people in my riding will know that I do not agree with their views.
First, I think the banks have done an exceptionally fine job. Any responsible person in a community can go to a bank and borrow money at a reasonable rate of interest. Far more people could and would borrow money from banks at this reasonable rate of interest, if it were not for the propaganda that has been spread across the country by people who have made speeches very similar to those we have heard in this House of Commons in the last two days.
The banks are good institutions: they are not bad institutions. They are good places from which to get money and with which to do business. They are good places from which to borrow money when it is found necessary to borrow money. And I just cannot understand the lack of consistency in the arguments offered by hon. members in the C.C.F. when at one time they condemn the banks and at another they say they are such great sources of revenue that the government should take them over. I think that is an inconsistency. If they are doing such a bad job, then surely the government should not be expected to take part in that bad job. If they are doing a good job, then why not allow the men who have done this good job to continue to do it.
Let me draw some comparisons between the banks and other institutions that lend money. I do not believe the average person should be encouraged to borrow money. That is not the policy my father taught me. In our house it was always considered dangerous to get into debt. And I think before the next ten or twenty years have passed it will be considered an unfortunate situation when a person is in debt. And when we hear it suggested loosely that we should borrow this, borrow that or borrow something else, I say it is very bad propaganda to be spread across the country from this House of Commons. But if a person does have to borrow money, surely the banks should not be criticized.
We have lending institutions in this country that charge as much as 24 per cent on many of their loans. And many of our citizens- far too many of them-are buying goods under those conditions. They will buy refrigerators and television sets in which they would have an investment of some $500
The Bank Act
or $600, and on this investment they would borrow as much as $500. In one year they will pay as much as $60 in interest charges on an average loan of $250. And when we find a rate of interest as high as 24 per cent, then I would highly recommend to the people who borrow at such a high rate that they consult their bankers, state what they are going to buy, and borrow the money at 6 per cent. Most of them could do this. There are not many people buying pieces of equipment of this kind who would be required to pay 24 per cent interest. Maybe our schools should educate our children to realize what their parents pay when they are confronted with the carrying charges demanded by finance companies in this country.
Some hon. members might be interested to know that many people who buy automobiles pay a higher rate of interest in carrying charges than they pay in the tax on those automobiles levied by the dominion government. On an automobile selling currently at around $3,000 the purchaser must pay at least $1,000 down. This means that he has to borrow $2,000, and usually this is spread over a period of 18 months. If this is done, the dealer would calculate his interest at 7J per cent on the $2,000 for a period of a year and a half. The interest that he would pay on the $2,000 would be $225. Thus the interest rate is 15 per cent. The tax he pays to the government on that same automobile is $469.
I suggest to people right across this country that they should stop and think before borrowing money at 15 or 20 per cent. We see the C.C.F. party, these socialists, coming out in condemnation of the banks. My recommendation to purchasers would be that they go to their banks and discuss the situation with bank managers. They will receive good advice and will be much farther ahead by getting the money through their bankers at a reasonable rate of interest than if they were to get it through finance companies.
This is one of the weaknesses of our day and age. People think it is quite all right to go out and pay rates of interest running up to 15 or 24 per cent on the articles they buy. My point is that if you borrow $2,000 you compute the interest at a rate of 7J per cent for the whole $2,000, and at the end of the year and a half there is nothing left of the amount borrowed, except perhaps one payment of $50. But he is still paying the interest computed on the $2,000 which he borrowed at first, and on the average amount borrowed the rate is 15 per cent. He pays 15 per cent on the actual money borrowed. I said he pays 7| per cent; that is a quick

The Bank Act
computation. It is actually 15 per cent that he pays when you consider he borrows $2,000 to start with and has nothing borrowed at the end of the year and a half. Therefore it is 15 per cent on the average amount of money borrowed. That is how it works out.
The only criticism I would make of the banks is of the service they offer to the people of this country. It is very difficult to go to most of our banks on Saturday in any of our large cities and borrow money. The only criticism I can find is that when they sell a service to the people of this country it is unfortunate that on Saturday, the one day when most people are free and should have access to the banks, the banks are not open. I do not think they should be criticized in the manner in which they have been, in this house in the past few days, because of that one weakness.
I would not want to suggest for one moment that I believe the people should borrow money. It is all right for businesses to borrow money because they intend to make more money with the money they have borrowed. But when a person borrows money in order to procure goods before he is in a position to pay for them, then he is paying far too much for those goods that he wishes to buy. If those individuals had the opportunity of approaching their bank managers and talking the situation over with them on Saturdays when they are off work they would find that the bank manager would generally give them the best advice that they could get. The banks could give a better service if they were open the whole week. But we realize that the bank employees should not have to work more days in the week than other people. Therefore we really cannot find much fault with them for closing one day in the week, which unfortunately happens to be Saturday, the same day that everyone else has off. We really cannot find too much fault with that.
We should encourage all the citizens of this country to deal with the banks, more particularly when they want to borrow money, because they will find that they will get a much better rate of interest from the bank than they will get from any other lending institution anywhere in the country.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking). In his opening remarks he said he did not think that the people should be borrowing money; that he was raised in a school where he was taught that he should pay cash on the line. Then he went on to say that the thing that worried him was that

the people were paying too high interest rates, and that they should borrow money from the banks. Therefore I really do not know whether he is for borrowing, against borrowing or just where he does stand. The ordinary consumer of this country will not gain much from the advice given him by the hon. member for Wellington South. He said he thought it was a mistake for people to go into debt to buy consumer goods. I do not think it is a mistake at all. It could be a mistake in given individual cases, but by going into debt for durable consumer goods people are able to make real savings by that means that they would not otherwise be able to make if they were endeavouring to put away a little cash from day to day until they got $400, shall we say, for a refrigerator.
I was astounded by the information he gave to the house that a great many people who buy automobiles pay more in interest charges than the automobile cost, and that happened under the regulations of the dominion government of which the hon. member is a part. Apparently thousands of people across Canada are allowed to buy automobiles, so the hon. member says, and the companies are allowed to charge such high interest rates that the charge for interest exceeds the price of the automobile. Perhaps that is so. If it is so, something should be done, and done immediately, to cut down the high interest rates.
