subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If I heard the hon. member incorrectly I withdraw the statement that those were his words. I wrote them down. If that is not his statement I shall let it go right here.
He went on to say that certain people were paying interest rates as high as 24 per cent. That is a shame, and the hon. member should be trying to influence the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to do something about it and to reduce the maximum interest rate that can be charged in Canada and stop the loan sharks charging legal interest rates up to 24 per cent a year. It is not just the little

finance company often off in the corner somewhere that charges high interest rates. The big retail companies, like Simpsons-Sears in Canada, charge interest rates of 15 per cent on what they call their budget plan. Those high interest rates demonstrate very clearly that today the banking system of Canada is falling down on the job, because if people could go to the banks and get the kinds of loans they want to buy durable consumer goods at 5 per cent or 6 per cent interest I am sure not one of them would be paying a rate of 15 or 20 or 24 per cent.
I read the speech of the Minister of Finance in introducing this measure, and the greatest weakness of the present proposal is the fact that the government, through its legislation in regard to chartered banks, has no program to prevent a recession, no program that I know of to increase the money in the hands of the consumers in Canada when we are facing a recession. Probably the Minister of Finance does not think we are facing a recession. I say we are in a recession now, and unless something is done about that recession very soon it may turn into a full-scale depression.
I am indebted to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) for having suggested to me that the speech from the throne in 1929 would make very interesting reading, the speech from the throne by a Liberal government. This is what the second paragraph says, as recorded at page 2 of Hansard of February 7, 1929:
The unprecedented prosperity which is apparent throughout the dominion affords cause for the deepest satisfaction.
That was in 1929. I continue:
Never in the history of Canada has there been such industrial and commercial expansion as that which has taken place during the past twelve months.
We have already heard that during this session. I continue:
The industry and enterprise of our people have been rewarded under Providence with an abundant harvest.
That's for sure right now.
In the production of agricultural and other basic industries all previous records have been surpassed. New records have also been established in the volume of construction and in the volume of foreign trade. Employment has been maintained at a high level and all indications point to a continuance throughout the country of the present favourable conditions.
Back in 1929 the government of the day, of the same political complexion as the present government, told the people of Canada that everything was fine, that production was high, that employment was high, that we had a wonderful crop; yet a few months later 83276-179
The Bank Act
we were in the depths of a depression. I hope we do not have anything like that again. But you will not prevent a depression by failing to recognize the signs that are very evident now that point to depression.
During the discussion on the resolution I expressed the belief that the banks usually followed the wrong practice in making loans as far as the interests of the country were concerned. In periods of inflation loans are usually easy to obtain, but in a period of declining prices the banks start to tighten their purse strings and the public find it very difficult to obtain loans. The banks, in spite of their assistance in averting a recession, by their action, assisted in bringing on a full-scale depression.
When we moved our amendment we did not expect to receive the support of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) or members of the Conservative party. We believe the banks should be nationalized, not because we think it is good to have more things being operated by the government, but because we say the history of the banks and banking practice in Canada demonstrates that the time has now arrived when, if certain objectives are to be achieved, the banks must be nationalized.
The government has used various methods of control but it is impossible, even with the best type of controls, to make the banks issue the type of loans which are in the best interests of the nation. Members of the Conservative party are in favour of leaving the banks under private enterprise because they say the banks should be in a position to take risks. But the banks are becoming less and less inclined to carry out that useful function, and the government very often has to give ironclad guarantees to the banks against loss. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), with the assistance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and other members of the cabinet, have to guarantee the banks against the loss even of a single dollar, then I believe it is time they acquired the right to take some direct responsibility for the lending policies of the chartered banks.
The government has given the banks certain guarantees which have induced the banks to make loans. One outstanding example is the guarantee to the chartered banks under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. That guarantee has certainly resulted in the banks making very substantial loans. In 1952 total loans made by the chartered banks under the Farm Improvement Loans Act amounted to $98 million. In other words the guarantee by

The Bank Act
the government against loss to the banks amounted to a total of almost $10 million. The total loss incurred by the banks and paid by the government for that year amounted to just a little over $12,000. To put it simply, the total loss for that year paid by the national treasury amounted to ylon of 1 per cent. Very little loss was entailed in making these loans, yet before the chartered banks would make loans available they had to have a guarantee that amounted to $10 million for the year 1952.
One could make the same type of comparison in regard to the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, and also in regard to the legislation approved the other day concerning housing.
We in this group would like to see the banks nationalized. We know perfectly well that this government will have nothing to do with the nationalization of the chartered banks. But members of the Liberal party have always professed support for cooperatives and claim that they believe in the co-operative principle. If that is the case they should be prepared to extend to the cooperative movement and to the credit unions the same kind of guarantee on farm improvement loans that is now given to the chartered banks in Canada. Our credit union movement is growing at a truly phenomenal rate. Credit unions now pay exactly the same kind of tax rate as any other corporation in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: The same as every corporation?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the kind of corporation my hon. friend is associated with wishes to pay exactly the same tax that is paid by the credit union, then that corporation can adopt different principles of management and their taxes will be precisely the same. If some of the private grain companies wish to pay dividends to farmers on the basis of patronage, as of course is done now, they can do that also.
The credit unions and other co-operatives pay exactly the same tax as any other business organization in Canada. I would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to a report on the credit unions in Canada for 1952 published by the marketing service of the Canadian Department of Agriculture. That report demonstrates the really tremendous growth of credit unions in Canada over the past ten years. In 1942 there were just under 300,000 members of the credit unions in Canada. By 1952 the membership had risen to 1,250,000, and in that year more than one out of every ten adult Canadians was a member of a credit union. The total assets of the credit unions in 1942 amounted to just under $44 million.

This figure had increased by 1952 to a total of $424 million. In ten years their assets have increased tenfold, and their membership by 300 per cent.
I believe the history of loans made by the credit unions in that ten-year period will compare favourably with the loans made by any of the chartered banks, with reference to losses sustained. I believe the government should give the credit unions exactly the same kind of guarantee it now gives the chartered banks. The government should not discriminate against the credit unions by giving the chartered banks a 10 per cent guarantee on farm improvement loans and no guarantee whatsoever to the credit unions who are engaged in a great many instances in exactly the same type of loan business.
The banks in Canada do not wish to take any risk in making loans. There are tens of thousands of Canadians who have gone to their bank, spoken to the bank manager, asked for loans, been turned down, gone to a credit union and obtained loans. In spite of the fact that many of the people dealing with credit unions are considered by the banks not to be good credit risks, nevertheless the history of the credit unions compares favourably with that of the banks in regard to losses sustained.
I wonder why the government has not given to the credit unions the same kind of guarantee it gives to the banks? Is it that the government does not want the credit union movement to expand at an increased rate over the years? Why are the banks any more deserving of guarantee by the government against loss than are the credit unions in Canada? I cannot understand why the government is not providing credit unions with exactly the same type of guarantee.
I notice that in the legislation before us this afternoon, as in the previous act, the banks are given the right to lend money to farmers on threshed grain. That is all very nice. The banks have the right to lend money on threshed grain, but the farmer has the problem of convincing the bank manager that he should be given a loan. If a farmer goes to a bank and asks for a loan on threshed grain, the banker will look to see if he owes any money in town, or if the farmer has a farm improvement loan from that bank. Unless the farmer can prove to the banker that he really does need a loan on his threshed grain, he will not get a loan.
The average farmer in Canada today- certainly that is so in western Canada- cannot get a loan on threshed grain. If he is a well-to-do farmer, with a huge quantity of grain on his farm, if he is out of debt, and if he has not delivered his quota he

may get a loan. But this section of the Bank Act is not being adequately utilized by the banks and for all practical purposes is not in operation at the present time.
When I began speaking I said that to my mind there was every indication that we are in a recession right now. Certainly the economy of western Canada is slowly grinding to a standstill. More and more businessmen are being forced to go on a cash basis. In this morning's Montreal Gazette there is a news report headed "Drake, Sask. Town Votes Out Credit". It reads as follows:
Drake, Sask., March 8.-Businessmen in this town 75 miles northwest ot Regina have voted to stop giving credit. The order is effective April 1.
R. E. Walker, a representative of the retail merchants association of Saskatoon, who addressed a meeting of merchants, said grain delivery quotas set by the Canadian wheat board are not large enough to take care of outstanding credit accounts. Merchants gave long-term credit to patrons but received only short-term credit from wholesalers.
From communications I have had from the retail merchants association and from businessmen in Saskatchewan it is fairly clear that this spring merchants will be going on a strictly cash basis. Anyone who is acquainted with farming operations in western Canada will realize just what a serious hardship that will mean to prairie agriculture.
I should like to see something done under this act, or some other appropriate steps taken, to put some cash in the pockets of farmers. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), members of parliament and everyone else who works likes to get paid. We all like to get paid, and to get paid on time. So does the wheat producer. He likes to produce wheat. That is what he is in business for. When he produces a crop, he thinks he should be able to get some money as a result of his efforts in producing that crop.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is always good at giving the farmers advice. On previous occasions he said to them, "Build granaries and store your wheat. Wheat on the farm is as good as cash in the bank". I have not yet met a farmer who would not like to get rid of the wheat he has and get some of the cash in the bank. The merchants in our towns would also like to get a little cash. I feel sorry for a farmer when he cannot sell his grain; but I think a merchant is even worse off, because he can get into trouble with his creditors very quickly when he has on his books a great many customers with outstanding accounts.
For financing this crop in western Canada I should like to see a method by which the farmer would not have to pay interest. I do not think doing it through the banks is
The Bank Act
the best way. But if the only way by which the government will provide the farmers with money is through the chartered banks, I say it is better to be done in that way than not at all.
I should like to see the interest rate kept at the very minimum. I think interest rates in Canada are too high today. I believe the government's policy of strengthening interest rates is wrong. I believe that policy should be reversed, and that steps should be taken to lower interest rates. I should like to see banks giving farmers loans at a nominal rate of interest. I believe they could do that if given a guarantee by the government. We had such guarantees at one time in the past, for the 1951 crop. The darkest picture the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) could paint-

speechtext:
I am just referring to the minister's statement at page 128 of Hansard. I cannot make a speech without bringing the minister into it somewhere, and probably this is as good a point as any at which to bring him in. At page 128 of Hansard he gave us some information as to the losses under that program. The minister's point was that the government's experience had not been good. I think the government's experience was good. The total amount the government can be liable for, as a result of that experience, is an amount not over 3 per cent of the aggregate loans. Most of those loans were made not for threshed grain but for grain out under the snow. If farmers will pay 97 per cent of their loans when obtained under those circumstances I believe they will pay, for all practical purposes, 100 per cent of any loans they may obtain for grain that has been threshed and is in storage.
We have in the act a section which allows the banks to lend money on farm-stored grain; but anyone from western Canada knows that very little money is being lent under that section. I therefore suggest that other steps must now be taken by the government or the economy of western Canada, going into a recession, will drag down the whole Canadian economy. We are losing markets-and we have lost a great many of them-for some of our most important grains. The farmer is looking for some money this spring. The merchants in western Canada need such a policy so the farmers can pay for the commodities they must obtain in order to continue their farming operations. Under this legislation I believe the government

The Bank Act
should be giving to the credit unions exactly the same type of guarantee it is now giving to the banks.
In another statement this session the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that it was his belief that now was the time for the government to loosen the purse strings. I agree with that statement. I think the government should loosen the purse strings at this time. As long as there are unemployed resources in the nation I do not agree that it is bad for the government to be spending large sums of money, more money than it collects through taxation. When there are half a million unemployed, when farmers are finding that their incomes are going down, that is the time for the government to adopt fiscal and monetary policies that will result in increased expenditures, an expansion of credit and an increase in the money supply so that our unemployed resources may be re-employed for the improvement of the standard of living of the Canadian people.

Is
the house ready for the question? The question is the following-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak now because my subject matter has to do with the amendment, and if the amendment is disposed of my subject matter will become more or less obsolete. Maybe I can finish in five minutes if I am not interrupted and if I can talk fast enough.
I have listened to the members of the C.C.F. group who have spoken on this matter, but I have failed to hear them suggest how they propose to nationalize the banking system. Therefore I want to ask them a question or two. I should like to ask them if they propose expropriation. If they do, that may follow the socialist line. I do not know. But if they do propose expropriation I am quite satisfied that the banks would contest it in the courts.
If it were contested what would the C.C.F. do? Would they dare tell the courts what decision they must make? If they did not dare to do that, then the courts would have to make the decision. If the courts decided to grant the petition of expropriation, then the decision would be appealed. If they failed to grant expropriation then the C.C.F. as a government would appeal the case.
We will suppose that the decision was in favour of expropriation. I fancy the matter would then be submitted to arbitration. Having been submitted to arbitration, the authorities who had to arbitrate would then have to determine a valuation. That valuation would involve the taking over of assets 
and capital stock, and I quite suppose it would also involve the taking over of the banks' cash reserves.
What would our socialist friends use with which to purchase all this? The cash reserves of the banks amount to about $900 million. The assets and capital stock of the banks amount to somewhere between $3 billion and $4 billion. They could not pay cash for them because the cash reserves of the banks constitute the only cash there is in the country. Therefore they could not pay cash. They could not get any cash in order to pay the banks under the settlement arrived at by arbitration. If they resorted to taxation they would have to tax the people to the extent of almost $1 billion to compensate for cash reserves alone.
Furthermore, here is one thing they would have to recognize. They would have to take over the liabilities of the banks. It is not generally recognized that every deposit that people have in the banks today is a liability against the banks. I should like to ask the C.C.F. whether they would take over the liabilities too, because if they did they would be taking over about $9 billion in liabilities. If they started this, what guarantee would they have against a run on the banks? This is a serious thing. They have not told us how they propose to do it.
In the minute I have left may I suggest that there is not a socialist country among the free nations of the world that has yet favoured nationalizing its banking system. Great Britain had a socialist government, but they did not venture it. Australia had a socialist government, but they did not venture it. New Zealand had a socialist government, but they did not venture it. Over the years we have heard a lot about the virtues of the government of Sweden. They did not venture it. Even the extreme national socialist government of Germany did not venture it. Our C.C.F. friends are proposing to do something that no socialist government has ever done. Why have they not done so? I believe these governments have recognized all that is involved, and have found that for all practical purposes it was impossible to do it. Someone behind me said something about McCarthyism. I do not know what that jab was for.

The house resumed, from Friday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hunter for the second reading of Bill No. 325, to authorize Niagara Gas Transmission Limited to construct, own and operate an extraprovincial pipe line.
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce):	Mr. Speaker, before I adjourned the debate when this measure was last before the house I pointed out that the government is unable to give the guarantee sought by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that the interests of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines will be protected. I pointed out that this measure is a private member's bill. The bill will be examined in the appropriate committee. It will then be returned here for third reading, and after the bill becomes law, all the decisions having to do with the project covered by this bill as well as the project covered by the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bill will be in the hands of the board of transport commissioners, whose decision will be final.
I stated at that time I had not had the pleasure of meeting an officer of the company. Since this bill has been under discussion I have had that pleasure. This afternoon I had a call from the general manager of Consumers' Gas Company, and as a result of our conversation, my information as to the intentions of the company is more complete. I now appreciate the fact that Consumers' Gas have realized that the Trans-Canada pipe line will be built, and that it has contemplated that an agreement must be made so that the two projects can work together.
The only reason any question is being raised about the bill before us is the thought that it may interfere seriously with the financing
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited and construction of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. In introducing the bill the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) stated that Consumers' Gas Company wishes to bring United States gas into the Toronto area. He stated that Consumers', through its subsidiary Niagara, now has a 20-year contract with the Tennessee Transmission Company covering the importation of some 23 billion cubic feet of gas annually. He also stated that subsequent arrangements have been made for Tennessee to repurchase all or any of this gas at any time for sale within the United States, should Consumers' Gas Company be in a position to purchase Canadian gas, without any loss to Consumers' Gas Company.
Assuming these arrangements are carried into effect, the Consumers' Gas Company will be able to supply the greater Toronto area with United States natural gas before the end of this year. Then the hon. member for Parkdale said that if and when Canadian natural gas becomes available the company will be in a position, without loss to themselves, to switch to Canadian natural gas. Obviously these are rather vague intentions vaguely stated. I feel we must have something more definite than the statement contained in the remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale before we can agree to the passing of this bill.
I think all hon. members realize that the Trans-Canada pipe line is a great conception. I suggest that this discussion should be entirely removed from politics. In the first place, a private member's bill should be considered apart from politics. If it were not I would be tempted to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) for having adopted Liberal policies with reference to oil and gas pipe lines. Since we are not talking politics, I shall refrain from doing so.

I point out that the government of Alberta is interested in the Trans-Canada pipe line, which will afford a badly needed outlet for the surplus gas of that province. The government of that province is co-operating with this government, and co-operating I think with the management of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
Saskatchewan is interested, of course, because the Trans-Canada pipe line will provide an outlet for gas which is already becoming surplus in that province, and which surplus is expected to grow in volume month by month. Manitoba is interested because it

Niagara Gas Transmission Limited would mean another competitive fuel in the province, which should greatly stimulate the growth of industry. Ontario is intensely interested in Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited for the reason that it promises an ample natural gas supply for all parts of the province as a competitive fuel. I would remind hon. members that Ontario now depends entirely on imported fuels for its energy other than hydroelectric energy. Quebec is interested for the same reason as Ontario. Therefore the great industrial areas of this country are vitally concerned with the building of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited project and with the additional energy that will be provided from that source.
It is a great project in another way. It is probably the greatest pipe-line project ever undertaken anywhere in the world. It is expected to cost around $300 million for the building of the pipe line. There will be gathering lines required in Alberta which will cost perhaps $50 million. Then chemical plants are required in Alberta to purify the gas before it goes through the pipe line. They will cost perhaps $100 million, and will provide an adequate supply of chemicals for industrial use in Alberta and throughout western Canada. In all the provinces concerned, there will be distributing systems and new apparatus for consuming gas. If everything is added up, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines represents a project running around $1 billion, all of which is to be spent before the year 1960.
The application for gas that is presently before the conservation board of the province of Alberta calls for a supply up to 540 million cubic feet of gas per day, whereas the bill before us calls for a supply of 23 million cubic feet of gas per day. Obviously the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines project is very much greater in concept than the project we are discussing. It is vital therefore to the interests of Canada, I believe, that there be no conflict between the two proposals. It would be tragic if the smaller proposal were permitted to interfere with the financing of the larger proposal. I believe, therefore, that this parliament must make sure that steps are taken so that interference will not occur.
There is a good deal of advantage to the larger project in undertaking the smaller project coupled with the proper safeguards. There are no very considerable markets for gas in eastern Canada built up at present, and such markets as there are have been built up to use manufactured gas. It would be very useful indeed if natural gas could be introduced into the Toronto area in volume


so that build-up could occur immediately and be well under way when western gas reaches Toronto. For that reason I think we must give sympathetic consideration to this bill.
Some will say there are other ways of effecting the build-up. We could perhaps draw on the natural gas reserves of western Ontario, which are considerable. But investigation has shown that the availability from that source would not be sufficient to accomplish the purpose. There is also a gas pipe line from the Detroit area bringing natural gas into the Windsor area at a very reasonable price. It is possible that that source of gas could be enlarged. But that would involve application to the federal power commission, and probably months of delay. I think that if the building of this proposed pipe line can be worked out on a basis that will protect the larger project, it may be a desirable step to take at this time.
Obviously, bringing gas in from Buffalo through a pipe line involves considerable investment, and one wonders what is to become of that investment if the line goes out of use in a matter of three years. I believe ways can be worked out so that investment can be assumed by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited; and I believe we should know, before this bill becomes law, that such an arrangement is being worked out to the mutual satisfaction of the Consumers' Gas Company and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.
Therefore I suggest that when this bill is before the committee, the committee will wish to examine the intentions of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited as well as the intentions of the Consumers' Gas Company Limited. And I believe it would be appropriate at that time to add another clause to the bill, a coming into force clause, which would provide that the bill would come into force at such time as a mutually satisfactory agreement between Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and Consumers' Gas Company can be deposited with the board of transport commissioners. This agreement would then be considered by the board of transport commissioners, and the date of coming into force would be the date of its approval by the board of transport commissioners. I believe this procedure would allow us to obtain the benefit that would be incidental to the building of this pipe line from Buffalo, and at the same time protect both the financial and the sales position of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I believe that this would represent a workable procedure for all concerned.
That is only my suggestion; there may be others. But I do think that to meet the

requirement laid down by the Leader of the Opposition-that the government should assure the house that the interests of the larger project will be protected-this may be as good a means as any for bringing about the protection asked for.

Mr. Speaker, the project envisaged by the bill has had a great deal of advertisement. I am surprised to find that the Consumers' Gas Company, which apparently has been in the red for so many years, should suddenly put on such an expensive advertising scheme, and apparently do it solely for the benefit of the people of Toronto. In all the advertisements I have read and received I note that the sole concern of Consumers' Gas Company is the welfare of its customers in Toronto. They point out that they are very anxious to get cheaper gas into that city before Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bring western gas to that community.
The sponsor of the bill tells us that this pipe line will probably be completed by the end of the year, and that gas from the United States will be delivered to Toronto customers by that time. I doubt this very much. I also note that the fuel controller in Ontario has said that we may possibly have western gas in Toronto via Trans-Canada pipe lines in about two years' time. If these statements are correct I fail to see where Toronto customers are going to receive such enormous benefits from the delivery of United States gas for one year; because, according to these statements, that will be the time between the delivery of United States gas and that delivered by Trans-Canada pipe lines.
I suspect that behind this movement there is an attempt on the part of Consumers' Gas Company to be in the distribution field when western gas arrives. There has been some comment in Ontario to the effect that the Ontario hydro might undertake the distribution of western gas in that province. The bill now before us would certainly place Consumers' Gas Company in a position where it would have facilities available for the distribution of gas not only in the metropolitan Toronto area but also in Hamilton and other points in the Niagara peninsula.
I may be wrong in my supposition, but I do say there should be some authority in Ontario in a position to tell us how western gas is to be distributed when it arrives, and the agency through which such distribution is to be made. If there is any possibility of the Ontario hydro becoming the distributing agency, I would be inclined to oppose the granting of this right to Consumers' Gas Company. I do not think advantages would be
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited gained by Toronto consumers that would warrant our handing over this public utility even to a limited dividend utility company, to the exclusion of the possibility of having the Ontario hydro or some other publicly-owned utility handling the distribution of this gas.
Certain it is that the necessary safeguards mentioned by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) must be taken before final approval is given to the bill. It is not enough, as the sponsor of this bill says, that there be an agreement between Consumers' Gas Company and the United States company to the effect that the United States company will undertake to buy all the gas Consumers' Gas Company may have contracted for when the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited line is completed. That is not sufficient. Before this bill receives final approval in this house I suggest that there must be a hard and fast agreement made and shown to the committee or made public to the effect that on the arrival of western gas via the Trans-Canada pipe line, that gas will be distributed in Toronto in lieu of the United States gas that will be brought in prior to the arrival of that pipe line.
I might say that more than the Progressive Conservative party is interested in this Canada-first policy as it applies to an all-Canada pipe line, notwithstanding the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on Friday to the effect that that policy was advocated by his party-and it was; there is no question of that. I simply want to add that other parties, including the C.C.F. and others, and members of the Liberal party as well, were just as ardent in their support of an all-Canadian pipe line as was the leader of the official opposition or the Conservative party. Certainly no steps must be taken at this time that will in any way interfere with or impede the progress of that Trans-Canada pipe line.
I would approve the suggestion made by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) that a clause be added to the bill which would enable the government or the board of transport commissioners to prevent this legislation from coming into operation until such time as satisfactory safeguards were provided to ensure that western gas would be distributed once the pipe line was completed into the Toronto metropolitan area. We should also add some understanding as to just what use is to be made of this pipe line from the Niagara boundary to Toronto when the Trans-Canada pipe line is built. Will this pipe line be used to transport Canadian gas from the main trunk lines to Hamilton, Welland and the Niagara peninsula, or is there

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the comments made today by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) and other hon. members. I may say that as a member from Alberta I am vitally concerned in seeing that Alberta and other western Canadian natural gas is sold as soon as possible and in as large a volume as possible; nevertheless I am strongly supporting this particular bill. My reasons for that I shall outline very briefly.
I believe that my community and my home province, like myself, are more vitally interested than any other part of Canada in getting markets for western Canadian natural gas as soon as possible and on the soundest possible economic basis. I realize, perhaps better than some of the proponents in this house of a strictly all-Canadian gas policy, that the policy they support must be substantially modified by the adoption of continental features in addition to purely national or nationalistic features.
That is, sir, this policy must be modified if Canada wants to achieve four things: First, the capture by Canadian gas of markets both here and in the United States big enough to absorb the expanding gas surplus in western Canada. For too long, both in my home province and in Ottawa, there have been expressions of fear concerning a gas shortage. The fear is of gas shortage for Canada's future needs, when our primary concern should be in blazing our way into markets, and with the much more serious problem of disposing of rapidly expanding gas surpluses.
Evidence was submitted by the Alberta conservation board a few months ago which dealt with the gas reserves proved up during the 18-month period to June 30 last, and in that province alone the increase in gas reserves over the period amounted to 4,700 billion cubic feet. In the meantime in British Columbia and Saskatchewan we have had other gas discoveries which bring gas reserve increases in western Canada to a rate exceeding 4,000 billion cubic feet in each 12-month period. This means that the gas found in each single year is adequate to supply one major pipe line for a period of 20 years. In other words, one year's discoveries in western Canada will provide eastern Canada, Ontario and Quebec, for a period of 20 years, and by the time we have the Trans-Canada pipe line in operation three years hence we will have enough natural gas resources in surplus to supply another two or three major pipe lines.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in our gas pipe-line planning we should deal with this project on a continental basis instead of piecemeal, as we have been doing by means

of private bills in this house for the last three or four years. We should have been concerning ourselves with what we were going to do with the continuing surpluses which are being built up in the west. I believe in a modification of this government's gas policy. If we are to achieve the capture of the nearest markets, first and fastest, regardless of the flag they wave, then that modification must be carried out in order that job and prosperity-creating gas field development and pipe-line construction can get under way as soon as possible in western Canada.
May I point out that during 1953 we had something of a recession in the gas exploration and development industry. Again, in connection with the modification of Canada's gas policy I feel certain this government and parliament will eventually approve an extension of natural gas supplies, regardless of their source, to as many Canadians as possible, as quickly as possible.
The fourth point in regard to the modification of Canada's gas policy, which I feel sure this parliament will accept, is that the policy should be so designed as to do the other things I have mentioned at a minimum of subsidy cost to the Canadian taxpayer. I feel, sir, that in our debates over the last two or three years on an all-Canadian pipe-line policy-and the blame for this must fall directly upon the minister in charge-we have argued about an all-Canadian gas system without any regard whatsoever to the economics involved. As regards the Trans-Canada bill which follows this one, let us argue it out against a background of public and parliamentary recognition that an allCanadian gas pipe line means accepting the principle of a subsidized pipe line.
I pointed out, sir, that we could, by redrafting our policy along correct lines, achieve the desired goal for Canada at a minimum cost to Canadian taxpayers. That is the major reason I am supporting this Niagara Transmission bill.
As a matter of fact, I believe that by immediately piping Louisiana gas by way of the Tennessee Transmission Company to the Consumers' Gas Company to service the people of greater Toronto, we will achieve four things. First of all, it will be the fastest method of getting natural gas to Toronto. It will mean the delivery of gas much sooner, providing parliament and the board of transport commissioners do not delay the implementation of this measure. It will mean the delivery of natural gas to Toronto at least two full years ahead of the earliest possible date of delivery of natural gas from western Canada.

Second, approval of this Niagara Transmission project would provide lower cost gas to the people of Toronto than could be supplied two years later from western Canada under a strictly all-Canadian policy. In addition, the approval of the Niagara project would cut the cost to Canada's taxpayers, the subsidy on an all-Canadian pipe line, by several million dollars.
Again, and this is perhaps most important at this time when we are faced with an unemployment problem in this country, the approval of this Niagara Transmission bill would create many hundreds of new jobs this spring in Ontario in the construction of the transmission pipe line and the construction of a distribution system through Toronto. It would also create many hundreds of jobs this year in the industries which manufacture the appliances through which the people would use the natural gas. All these jobs would be provided this year instead of in 1956 or 1957, when the all-Canadian pipe line comes through. Approval of this bill will provide jobs for those who will distribute these appliances throughout the Toronto area and in the east generally. It will provide an immediate means of creating jobs without government handouts.
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated that there are some phases of the all-Canadian gas policy with which I do not agree. The house is well aware of my views in this matter. I am not going to belabour them now, because when the Trans-Canada pipe-line bill comes before the house that will be the proper time to discuss and debate the broader aspects of a Canadian gas policy. Mr. Speaker, this pipe line and the many others on which this house has passed legislation in the past couple of years have been referred to by many hon. members as national pipe lines. I want to say that the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) a few moments ago on this bill proves that they are not national pipe lines. In reference to this bill, the minister set out the fact that there were safeguards and that a clause would be placed in it which would prevent the operation of the legislation until all the evidence was taken. But going on a little bit further, he said that Manitoba was interested in this bill as were Ontario, Quebec and Alberta; and that ended Canada.
May I say that there are four provinces east of Quebec that are greatly interested in these pipe-line bills, but for a different reason. They are not going to make any money out of them, and they are not going to get any cheap fuel out of them. The whole objective of this and the other bills, as far as Ontario and Quebec are concerned, is directed toward one thing, namely to get cheap fuel regardless of the repercussions in any other part of the country. I expected the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) to be on his feet objecting to this bill because it, as well as others like it, are creating headaches for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys at the present time.
Only last evening the minister had a delegation from Nova Scotia wait on him in reference to a mine closing for lack of markets. Of course he told them he could not do anything about it. He sent them on to Montreal to meet with the heads of the Canadian National Railways. On the 12th of this month the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys again will be meeting a delegation from Nova Scotia consisting of representatives of the mine workers' union and the heads of the operating coal industry in that province. Their purpose in going to see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is to determine the future of the coal industry of that province. The problem in the province is what? It is that of markets. Why are they afraid of expanding the industry or developing it? Because there is a threat from natural gas and oil.
While I have no objection to Ontario getting cheap fuel, I am blaming the government for not having a national fuel policy that is allembracing, whereby a study would be made of the whole question of fuels. Then gas or oil would be piped into the areas where it was most economic to do so, having due regard to the provincial economies that are based on other fuels and are going to be wiped out when these gas and oil developments are fully implemented.
The thing that irks me is this. Every time a member gets to his feet in the house he figures that if you can serve Quebec and Ontario from the western provinces, that is a national project.

When the hon. member says that the discussion of a national fuel policy is not relevant to this bill, I suggest that he had better do a little bit of studying on the problem; and if he does so, I think he will find that it is relevant.
As I was pointing out, in all these discussions I have never yet heard any member of this house suggest that there was any problem east of Quebec in connection with this natural gas question. I was a member of the committee that considered the first natural gas bill to be introduced in the house. At that time I asked the witnesses who appeared before the committee whether they had made any survey east of Quebec, and they admitted they had not. No consideration whatsoever had been given. As I was pointing out when I was interrupted, there are four provinces east of Montreal, and the threat of natural gas and oil is creating the problem so far as coal is concerned. Delegations are coming to Ottawa to meet with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to determine whether there is any solution to the problem.
This bill is to be sent to a committee, and I suggest to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) that when it goes there an examination should also be made of the repercussions on the whole maritime economy by virtue of the fact that in this house we are passing bills-with very little consideration, in my judgment-to provide for the piping of natural gas and oil from western Canada. It is not a question of considering natural gas or oil alone; but rather it is one that is related to the matter of other fuels. Unless an examination is made from the point of view of a national fuel policy, one of these days we are going to find ourselves with an emergency on our hands. We will find that fuels going into certain areas are needed somewhere else and for some other purpose. Mines are being closed indiscriminately across Canada today, and we are not going to be able to open them up the moment we need that fuel.

Niagara Gas Transmission Limited
I think it is almost time someone took a look at the question. The statement was made that this gas development is a billion dollar project which will bear full fruit about 1960. That is a lot of money. It is a big investment, and I should think those who are investing that money would sit down and take a look at the whole fuel question before that amount of money is invested. Only last night in Montreal the president of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, one of the biggest organizations in Canada, said that in the maritime provinces coal, steel and textile areas were depressed today. It is getting pretty bad when he will make such a statement, because he has always taken the other view.
We are asked to pass a bill that will make natural gas available to the province of Ontario and ultimately to the province of Quebec. Natural gas will replace coal for all domestic purposes and also in industry in Canada, with the exception of basic steel. When it is said that by 1960 this billion dollar program will be fully developed it means that natural gas will be supplying the whole area of Quebec and Ontario. It also means that the whole coal industry of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is going to be a casualty in the path of technological advance.
The government has some responsibility to the four maritime provinces that depend to a large extent on coal. We also have some responsibility to them. What is going to happen then? Are no benefits to accrue to that part of the country as the result of this investment in gas and oil, and the money the federal government is going to spend in these projects?

I think the province of Saskatchewan has set an example in the field of natural gas. Private industry is developing the wells but the Saskatchewan government has set up a crown company to distribute the gas. The crown company there that is doing this job is also the company that is concerned with hydroelectric power. They are in the field of fuel, and are planning natural gas development in the Saskatchewan area in the way that will be most economic. It is not being done haphazardly as we are doing here by granting franchises for pipe lines all over the country, to pipe Canadian gas across the border into the United States and to pipe United States gas


across the border into Canada. If we are going to break down trade barriers on this continent in order to supply the province of Ontario with natural gas it is pretty nearly time we began to wipe out trade barriers all along the line.
If Ontario thinks it is good business to bring in cheap natural gas from across the line, then it is just as good business for Ontario and the four maritime provinces to be able to get cheap automobiles and not have to pay a tariff of 25 per cent on them. About 35 per cent is added to the cost of everything imported from the United States that the maritime consumer eats and wears, by the time it is hauled across the country to him. If we are going to start knocking down barriers in order to have cheap fuel, let us start knocking them down for everything else right down the line. You cannot retain trade barriers in order to protect central Ontario manufacturers for certain purposes, and knock them down for another purpose because benefits will accrue to the central provinces. If Ontario is going to take natural gas and distribute it, then in my opinion the body already in the field of fuel, the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission, is the organization that should control the distribution, because I believe they can plan it in a much better way than some pipe-line company which merely wants to pipe it in there for the purpose of making money.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OP CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to propose one specific change in the Bank Act tonight, Mr. Speaker, a change that has to do with agriculture. It seems to me that one of the major gaps or major weaknesses in our banking system over the past few years has been its failure to provide adequate long-term credit facilities for farmers. The banks seem to feel, and I admit with some justification, that marginal

farmers, because of climatic conditions, because of uncertainties of price and markets, are perhaps not good credit risks. As a result Canadian farmers, no matter in what province they live, seem to have difficulty today in obtaining long-term credit.
A few days ago this particular problem was discussed in the Saskatchewan legislature during the debate on a private member's resolution. According to a Canadian Press dispatch of last Thursday, the resolution, and I quote-
. . . asked the federal government to set up a lending agency to provide loans to young farmers starting out or extend limitations of present lending agencies.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that resolution pinpointed the problem which should be considered by the banking and commerce committee when this particular act is being reviewed. The lack of long-term agriculture credit facilities in my opinion is having a harmful effect on our economy and is causing unnecessary trouble for farmers. As every hon. member knows, no matter from what province he comes, in recent years there has been a steady and persistent drift of farmers into the cities. I think one of the reasons for this trend is to be found in the fact that they are finding it ever more difficult to become established on the farms. The price of land today has skyrocketed. The price of machinery is becoming ever higher, and it is very costly for a young farmer to purchase a basic herd of cattle or of livestock.
In western Canada today if a young farmer wants to start out on a half section of good land, with all the equipment to farm it, it costs him roughly $20,000. Such a figure, of course, is out of reach of about 90 per cent of our farmers. There is no place where they can obtain adequate credit to purchase such a farm. As a result, I say again that many of these young farmers have left the rural areas and drifted into the city. It is quite true, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) pointed out the other day, that the federal government has within the past few years set up the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
I want to say at once that both of these acts have been extremely beneficial. However, I believe most hon. members will admit that the provisions of these acts have been found to be too limited in scope. Trying to qualify for loans, most farmers either find the down payment required under these acts too high, or the proposed security required too severe, or the amount which could be borrowed too small. For instance, if my memory serves me correctly the ceiling in the farm improvement act is $4,000. When
The Bank Act
you realize that today in western Canada a tractor alone costs perhaps $3,000 and a combine about $6,000, most hon. members will realize that the ceiling is too low.
Thus I say that experience has shown the provisions of both the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act are completely inadequate to provide farmers with the type of credit which they need today. It seems to me the time has come for this parliament to remedy that weakness while we are discussing the banking system.
I suggest there are several methods which could be used. In the first place, the provisions of the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act could be extended, the ceilings could be elevated and so on. Parliament might also consider a second alternative. In this Bank Act, if I understand it correctly, the minister is proposing that the banks should be guaranteed by the government against losses on 20 to 30-year loans which they make to urban dwellers on the construction of new homes. Why would it not be feasible, under this act, to give the banks similar guarantees against losses which they might have in making 20 to 30-year loans to farmers for the purpose of purchasing new farms or new equipment?
As I see it the principle would be the same in both cases. In that way the farmer could obtain the long-term credit which he so badly needs in Canada today without undue expense being placed upon the taxpayers. If the banks are prepared to accept long-term mortgages on houses under a government guarantee, I believe they should be prepared also to accept long-term farm mortgages under the same type of guarantee.
I may say that I have discussed this matter with bankers I know, and they cannot see any particular flaw in the argument. I realize, of course, that certain safeguards would have to be established so the banks' liquid position would not be jeopardized. I say again, Mr. Speaker, I think the time has come for this parliament to do something to provide the kind of credit facilities that our agriculture needs. I have suggested these two methods, and if there is something wrong with them I hope the Minister of Finance will tell me precisely what it is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister recalls the discussion we were having in respect of clause 431 the last time the committee dealt with the Criminal Code. Is the minister awaiting his assistants?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
As he may recall, some of us were concerned as to this clause. It is a new one and it seemed to me on the previous occasion we discussed it, and still seems to me, that its provisions grant rather wide authority. It makes it possible for one who is armed with a warrant for the seizure of certain things to seize other articles in addition to those set out in the warrant if, in the opinion of the peace officer who has the warrant, there are grounds for so doing.
I listened with interest to what the minister had to say on this matter on February 26, but I must say I was more impressed by what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings had to say, particularly when he pointed out that the wording of a warrant can usually be made wide enough to embrace any of the articles involved in a particular offence. As the minister knows, it has been my concern and the concern of some other hon. members in

this house in going through the code that we do not go too far in the direction of providing peace officers with too much authority without a warrant being properly drawn.

subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I amplify what I said in committee the other night when we were dealing with this clause. I feel it is necessary because my hon. friend has merely summarized the discussion, and frankly I believe the minister will have some difficulty in providing justification for this clause. It will be observed that clause 431 contains within it reference to clause 429. Clause 431 reads:
Every person who executes a warrant issued under section 429 may seize, in addition to the things mentioned in the warrant, anything that on reasonable grounds he believes has been obtained by or has been used in the commission of an offence, . . .
-and so on. But, Mr. Chairman, if you go back to clause 429 you will find provisions
(a), (b) and (c) are so wide that they include almost everything under the sun. To use a colloquial expression, they include everything but the kitchen sink. Paragraph (a) of clause 429 reads:
(a)	anything upon or in respect of which any offence against this act has been or is suspected to have been committed.
And then paragraphs (b) and (c) read:
(b)	anything that there is reasonable ground to believe will afford evidence with respect to the commission of an offence against this act, or
(c)	anything that there is reasonable ground to believe is intended to be used for the purpose of committing any offence against the person for which a person may be arrested without warrant.
It must be remembered that the information will be preferred by a skilled officer, perhaps of the R.C.M.P. or other branch of the police, and that this is not a warrant for the arrest of an individual where the charge is limited specifically. In such cases a peace officer cannot go beyond that charge; otherwise he would be guilty of complicity and the warrant or the indictment would become void. This is information upon which a search warrant will be taken out and within which the officer responsible, I suggest with all due deference, can include everything which any reasonable person could anticipate.
Having done that, it is not necessary to use the provisions of clause 431, unless by any chance the officer has been lax or careless, in which case I frankly do not believe we should require in the Criminal Code a clause which is quite so wide as this. Under this provision, if the officer has forgotten or fails to include within the information everything from Dan to Beersheba, he can in addition to the one thing mentioned in the
Criminal Code
warrant seize anything be believes on reasonable grounds has been used in that offence.
For example, Mr. Chairman, I can imagine a husband or wife buying a washing machine and stating that they can pay $10 per month, when actually their earning power is considerably exaggerated. It would then be perfectly conceivable under this clause for the vendor to seize that washing machine, because he could claim that the buyers obtained it by falsely representing their income, and that in fact they lacked the purchasing power.
I certainly do not want a situation of that kind created, and I know the Minister of Justice would be the first to oppose such a development. But I am saying to him with all the force I can command that if this clause is permitted to stand as it now is, then it will be open to a great many abuses, and we will find the Criminal Code being used for the seizure of goods which should actually be recovered under civil procedure, if they are seized at all.
I would be the first to admit that we should not handicap an officer of the law, and that we should provide him with all necessary powers; but I do not like umbrella clauses, or general catch-alls such as we have here. I know the minister will give an explanation which will undoubtedly appeal to reason, but I would also suggest with all due deference that if he were sitting on this side of the house, I would hate to think how much time he would take in opposing the enactment of the clause we have before us now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I think I should address myself to the last point made by my hon. friend, but first let me deny as emphatically as I can that in the improbable event of my sitting on the other side of the house I would oppose this clause. I am not supporting it merely because I am sitting on this side of the house. I am supporting it because I think it is a necessary provision to have in the bill.
I went to some considerable length in outlining the justification for this clause on the last occasion on which it was before the committee, and I do not believe it is necessary for me to cover the same ground tonight. However, I should deal with the points raised by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. He claims that if this clause is passed it will enable a creditor to seize, say, a washing machine.

subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: It is possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Yes, but I would suggest that he look carefully at clause 429, under which the warrant has to be issued. When my hon. friend talks about subsection (a), covering

Criminal Code
anything upon or in respect of which any offence against this act has been or is suspected to have been committed-and the same sort of provision is in (b) and (c)-I think he will agree from his own experience that in order to get a search warrant under section 429 at all the informant has to satisfy the justice that he believes, upon reasonable grounds, that an offence has been committed.
When he establishes that by his information, then the information is issued only in respect of things which have to do with that offence. The warrant only applies to things under
(a), (b) or (c) in relation to that offence. It does not make any difference how broad
(a), (b) and (c) are. The restriction does not arise under these subsections. It arises from the fact that when the warrant is issued it is in respect of a certain offence which is disclosed in the information sworn before the justice. I see that my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings is nodding his head in assent to that statement, and I am glad he agrees with what certainly is the case.
When the peace officer has this warrant, he goes to the place where he thinks he is going to find the property which was involved in that offence which was referred to in the information and in the warrant that is in his possession. When he gets there, he discovers that this particular thief has been active in more spheres than anyone had suspected, and that he not only has all of the swag from this particular offence but a lot of material from perhaps several other offences as well. This is not an imaginary situation. Time after time we see in the newspapers reports to the effect that when the police went to seize under a search warrant of this sort they found goods that had been stolen in a series of robberies in that community over a previous period of time.
What my hon. friends of the opposition are arguing is that under a set of circumstances such as that, the peace officer should solemnly seize the articles covered by the warrant he has, as being those that were connected with the offence in respect of which the warrant was issued; and then, so far as all the other ones are concerned, he says, "Well, I have not any authority to do that. I shall go back to the magistrate and see if I can get some more warrants to cover these other matters". Is that common sense?
I had perhaps better not ask my friend the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings the rhetorical question, "Is that common sense"; I shall merely say that it does not seem to me to be common sense. It is only after the peace officer has been armed with the warrant in respect of a particular offence disclosed in a sworn information before the justice, and he goes and finds ether goods

which upon reasonable grounds he believes to have been the subject matter of other offences, that he has any right to take them. To my mind this section is an improvement in this part of the code.

subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
With all deference, may I say this. We are not going to involve the minister in rhetorical questions or otherwise. He was suggesting that perhaps I was not talking common sense. Perhaps I am not prepared to offer an opinion because I might be slightly prejudiced.
Nevertheless I suggest, with all deference, that the minister has not met the point I raised. In other words, he says that section 429 deals with a specific offence. It is certainly possible for any embryonic lawyer or any embryonic police officer to draw up an information under section 429 which would be wide enough to cover any possible eventuality that might occur.
I am not going to waste the time of the committee by stressing this point again, having done it once. My complaint is not that anything might be done under section 429; but having laid the information, we come back and find that it is any person who can do this. Mind you, it need not be a police officer; this can be anybody. You are not limited to a peace officer. You are not limited to a constable. And even some of these people, I am rather afraid, have fearful ways of dealing with matters. I am just thinking of a peace officer who was on traffic duty in a city not too far away from here when a horse dropped dead in what was known as Confederation square. It was not Confederation square in Ottawa, I may say. He could not spell "confederation" so he unharnessed the horse and dragged it till he came to Prince street, which was his own name and he could spell it. Then he filled in the traffic report saying that he found the horse on Prince street. That sort of thing sometimes happens with peace officers.
You are going beyond even that class now. You are saying that any person who executes a warrant may seize things in addition to the things mentioned in the warrant. I say again with all emphasis-and I am not stressing it further-that everything should be mentioned in the warrant that could possibly be included within the scope of any particular crime with which you were concerned. If you are going on a fishing expedition I think you should at least fish within the ambit of the law, and not under a general umbrella. You add that to the fact that any person can do that, that he can seize anything. It might be a bootlegging offence. As I say, it might be something resulting from credit.

The minister says this is an improvement in the law. Possibly it is, Mr. Chairman. But I simply point out that the criminal law of this country has been fairly well administered since confederation, and the Criminal Code has been a fairly effective instrument of legislation. There are hon. gentlemen in this house who have been connected with its enforcement. For instance, there is the hon. member for Cumberland sitting on my right, who for years has been a crown prosecutor in his own constituency, and there are many others in this house who have had similar experience. It seems to me rather strange that we now find this new section being drafted which in my opinion, at any rate, goes farther than the code went previously.
I always object to the law being stretched to the limit. I think we must, as far as possible, maintain the old concept of specific offences, specific crimes and specific informations. I am not going to urge the matter further but I do say that I think this is not an improvement. I say that with all respect to the minister. He can refer to section 429 as much as he likes, but I am sure that any officer who is retained by the Department of Justice and lays an information which does not bring the matters which the minister wants investigated within the scope of that section, will not be retained a second time, unless there is a great deal of pressure brought to bear upon the minister. It is only when they fail to do that that you are back within the provision of this section. I say it is unnecessary and I say it is unwise; and I at least want to register my own objection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
No. I think there is another objection to this clause, Mr. Chairman, on the ground that in none of these sections so far as I can see is any time limit laid down within which a warrant must be executed. That may be a non-essential. When you act under clause 431 and seize anything else in addition, that is one thing. When you read that in conjunction with clause 432 (3) (a), under which the magistrate or the justice is now to be the judge of whether or not the thing was lawfully in possession of the person from whom it was seized, you have three things. It is not included in the warrant. It is seized on the suspicion of some peace officer that it was obtained unlawfully. Yes; my friend the hon. member for London corrects me and says it may not be a peace officer, but may be seized by any person who fancies that it was obtained by the commission of an offence. Then after it has been seized and is before the justice, that
Criminal Code
justice, without any sort of trial, if he thinks it was obtained unlawfully orders it to be forfeited. Then added to all these considerations is the fact that no time limit is specified within which this extraordinary power may be exercised. I think it is going much too far, and I would certainly propose to vote against the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I wonder if, while we are on this section, I might bring to the attention of the members of the committee a representation which I have received from Mr. N. A. Munnoch, general counsel of the Bell Telephone Company. He had made representations before the special committee of the House of Commons last year in connection with this same question. Mr. Munnoch refers to section 171, subsection 6 of the bill, which hon. members will find on page 57. That is the section authorizing a search warrant in connection with gaming houses.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: We are back to the corner stores again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
No, not to the corner stores. This is a different kind of gaming house. This is a gaming house where a lot of telephone lines have been installed in order that those in charge may receive and place bets on race tracks. The complaint of the telephone companies, on the strength of which this subsection was placed in the code previously, was that when the police came in they took the telephones in the course of seizing exhibits and ripped them from the walls, and in doing so frequently damaged them severely. To meet that situation it was provided by subsection 6 of section 171 that-
Nothing in this section authorizes the seizure, forfeiture or destruction of telephone, telegraph or other communication facilities or equipment owned by a person engaged in providing telephone, telegraph or other communication service to the public or forming part of the telephene, telegraph or other communication service or system of such a person.
Before the House of Commons committee Mr. Munnoch represented that clause 431, which we are now discussing, might have this effect of permitting and I think I had better use his words rather than paraphrase them-
... "a person, armed with a search warrant pursuant to section 429, to seize telephone, telegraph and other communication facilities and equipment if, on reasonable grounds, he believed they had been used in the commission of an offence, despite the fact that they are exempt from seizure under section 171. This would seem to conflict with and nullify, or to a large extent impair, the protection given to communication companies by section 171.
In order to remedy this situation and give such companies the protection to which they are, in my submission, entitled, I respectfully suggest that

Criminal Code
either section 431 be amended by adding a provision substantially similar to that contained in subsection 6 of section 171 or that subsection 6 of section 171 be amended by adding after the word "section" in the first line thereof, the words "or in section 431", so that the said subsection would read as follows:
"(6) Nothing in this section or in section 431 authorizes the seizure, forfeiture or destruction of telephone, telegraph or other communication facilities or equipment owned by a person engaged in providing telephone, telegraph or other communication service to the public or forming part of the telephone, telegraph or other communication service or system of such a person."
The House of Commons committee rejected that argument, and when we were considering introducing the code last fall I advised Mr. Munnoch that we were going to introduce it-with the few minor exceptions I have called to the attention of hon. members, typographical errors and the like-in substantially the same form as that in which it had emerged from the House of Commons committee of last year. He then asked me if, when we came to clause 431, I would be good enough to present to this committee and myself endorse these representations of his which I have just finished quoting. I said I could not endorse them, because my view was that we should adhere to the decision that had been made by the House of Commons committee, but that I would bring the matter to the attention of hon. members of this committee as I have now done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
